speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Of the 19 non-Budget proposed tax changes, eight changes are proposed refinements to the income tax regime while the remaining 11 changes are technical amendments to remove obsolete provisions or to provide clarifications on the law.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We sought views from the public on the draft Bill from 20 June to 11 July 2018.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Ministry of Finance (MOF) evaluated all the feedback received and incorporated them where relevant to the draft text of the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will help companies, especially smaller ones, cope with near-term cost pressures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 43 and 44 of the Bill provide for this change.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, adjustments will be made to the Start-Up Tax Exemption (SUTE) Scheme and the Partial Tax Exemption Scheme from YA 2020.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The tax exemption under both schemes will be reduced from the first $300,000 to $200,000 of normal chargeable income.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Exemption under the SUTE Scheme will also be lowered from 100% to 75% for the first $100,000 of normal chargeable income.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Even with these changes, corporate tax will remain low for startups and smaller companies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In addition, startups and smaller companies can tap on a wide range of Government support measures to build capabilities and grow their businesses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, clauses 32(f), 50(a) and 50(d) to (g) of the Bill provide for these changes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This enhanced deduction will be available from YA 2019 to YA 2025.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 16 and 17 of the Bill provide for the change.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And clauses 14 and 19 of the Bill provide for this change.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They give effect to the announcements that were made in Budget 2018 this year.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As mentioned earlier, MOF also regularly reviews and refines the income tax regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, I will now highlight the three broad changes arising from this periodic review of the tax regime which are in the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, we will enhance the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore's (IRAS') powers to investigate tax crimes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Tax offenders and criminal syndicates are becoming more obstructive and employing more sophisticated schemes to defraud the authorities and cover up their crimes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, IRAS has powers to require persons to provide information, record statements and take possession of documents or items that constitute evidence of tax offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Enhanced investigative powers are required to more effectively deal with serious tax offenders, as well as acts of obstruction which may hamper IRAS' investigations and prosecution.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Such obstructive acts include taking flight, destroying or refusing to hand over evidence, and contacting other witnesses to collude or fabricate evidence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The proposed amendments will enhance IRAS' investigative powers, by providing authorised IRAS officers with the (a) power of forced entry; (b) power to arrest without warrant; and (c) power to carry out body search; subject to conditions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I will refer to these as enhanced investigative powers in my speech.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I should also note that investigation officers of other tax authorities, such as the United Kingdom (UK) and the United States (US) have similar powers to facilitate their investigations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will put in place safeguards in the way these enhanced legislative powers are exercised.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, the power to arrest without a warrant may only be exercised for an investigation of serious tax offences, such as tax evasion, or where a suspect attempts to destroy evidence with a view to hindering or obstructing IRAS' investigations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The power of forced entry may only be exercised if entry cannot be gained to a building or place in two situations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One, when it is for an investigation of a serious tax offence and there is reason to believe that there is in a place an item relevant to the investigation or prosecution that may otherwise be concealed, removed or destroyed, Or, two, when there is a reason to believe that a person liable to be arrested under the Act is in the building or place.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The power to carry out a body search may only be exercised on a person found in a place which IRAS has lawfully gained entry into for the purpose of investigating a tax offence and to search for items which may be relevant for investigation or prosecution.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There is an additional safeguard for a woman to only be searched by a female officer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: All these enhanced investigative powers may only be exercised by officers authorised by the Comptroller of Income Tax.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These authorised officers would receive training consistent with those in other law enforcement agencies, such as Singapore Customs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The amendments will also expand IRAS' power to gather all information relevant to its investigations or prosecution of tax offences from any person.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Currently, IRAS may gather information relating to a person's income, assets or liabilities only.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The amendment will allow IRAS to gather all information as long as it is relevant to the investigation or prosecution.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, this could include information relating to business transactions or information relating to accomplices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In addition, the amendments will align the penalties imposed under the Income Tax Act for persons who obstruct officers acting in discharge of their duty with those for a similar offence under the Goods and Services Tax Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Specifically, section 66 of the Goods and Services Tax Act imposes a maximum fine of $10,000 and imprisonment of up to 12 months, or both, for obstruction of officers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 2(b), 3, 41, 42, 45, 46 and 47 of the Bill provide for all of the changes which I have just described.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Serious crimes are offences listed in the First and Second Schedules to the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We need the proposed amendments as the activities of criminals, including syndicates, are often multifaceted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Their criminal activities may not be limited to tax evasion and may extend to other forms of illegal activities like drug dealing and corruption.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A whole-of-Government approach is required to better tackle such serious crimes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Again, I would highlight that other countries, including Australia, Norway, Sweden and the UK, also allow for the disclosure of tax information to LEAs to combat non-tax crimes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Under the proposed amendments, information shared is to be disclosed by the Comptroller to the head of an LEA for the purpose of investigation or prosecution of serious crimes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Unauthorised onward disclosure of such information would constitute an offence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And clause 4 of the Bill provides for the changes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Third, we propose to amend the Income Tax Act to allow tax deduction for motor car-related expenses for private hire car (PHC) drivers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Unlike taxi drivers, PHC drivers are currently not allowed to claim tax deduction on car-related expenses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have reviewed this issue with the Ministry of Transport (MOT) and taken into account feedback from various Members of Parliament during debates on this matter as well as the National Private Hire Vehicles Association.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Such expenses would include car rental and petrol, for example.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The ratio is a proxy for all expenses incurred to earn driving income, including service fees paid to platform providers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Alternatively, the PHC driver may opt to claim tax deduction based on the actual amount of expenses incurred in earning driving income.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, they can opt for the deemed 60% deduction or they can claim tax deduction based on the actual amount of expenses incurred.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The convenience of a deemed expense ratio will be extended to taxi drivers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Like PHC drivers, taxi drivers will be allowed to opt for the deemed expense ratio to ease tax compliance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Alternatively, taxi drivers can choose to continue with their current practice of claiming tax deduction based on the actual amount incurred on relevant expenses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Capital allowance for the purchase costs of cars will continue to be disallowed for PHC drivers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As for taxi drivers, almost all currently do not own their taxis and, therefore, do not claim capital allowance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For taxi drivers who own these yellow-top taxis, the capital allowance in respect of their taxis will be grandfathered.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These changes in tax treatment update our tax regime to allow deduction for car-related expenses incurred by PHC drivers, while maintaining support for our long-standing policies on car ownership under our tax regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clauses 22, 23 and 24 of the Bill provide for the changes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And, in spite of various issues enshrouding PHC, the demand for their services has not abated.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If at all, demand has, in fact, increased, and this is especially so for families with elderly and young children; and, also for those with less mobile family members, as maneuvering around with buses and trains still has its challenges.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The convenience of almost door-to-door service, and with a driver to assist those on wheelchair, PHC is a good option.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, PHC drivers provide a necessary transportation service for the public.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They complement taxi drivers or compete with our taxi drivers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It depends on how you look at it.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, PHC drivers deserve to claim tax deductions and receive fair remuneration for their labour.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And that is why I spoke on this issue in Parliament before.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And now, they should be happy to hear about this amendment.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They say that some of the PHC drivers are full-time drivers; some are part-time drivers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, how is IRAS going to differentiate between these two categories of claims?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For fuel claims, I think that is quite straightforward as mileage clocked for ferrying passengers will be recorded by the PHC's platform.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But for parking and rental, it is next to impossible to identify how much of these expenses go into picking up passengers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And, once some PHC drivers are approved to provide courier services, there will be further blurring of lines between work and personal.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Undoubtedly, some PHC drivers are full-time drivers, and it would be somewhat unfair to deprive them of the same tax benefits as full-time taxi drivers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: PHC platforms are enhancing their services to meet the needs for more courier services.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the meantime, we are seeing more ad hoc couriers on our roads.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These are people who drive their own vehicles from cars, vans to motorcycles.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They pay for parking and, in the case of motorcyclists, they have to pay for high motorcycle Certificates of Entitlement (COEs), all of which come out of their own pockets.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: These are issues that I have already brought up in Parliament previously.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I think it is important that the Government recognise this trend and review the regulatory framework for this sector, including having an appropriate income tax regime for all these operators.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   It is a good idea to give tax deduction to PHC drivers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, PHC drivers are different from taxi drivers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If the driver drives his car mostly for personal use, he could abuse the tax benefits.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, people who use their own vehicle to provide courier services must pay for parking and a high motorcycle COE.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: To be fair, they should also enjoy tax benefits.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: To begin, I would like to express my appreciation that MOF has been responsive to public feedback to simplify and increase the allowed tax deduction on car-related expenses incurred by PHC drivers.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Tax simplification is always welcome, both to promote compliance as well as to improve the efficiency of administration and enforcement.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: And that is how we typically think about the gig economy worker – a self-employed person, an independent contractor, and not an employee protected by the Employment Act.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: In fact, the Tripartite Workgroup Report whose recommendations on gig economy workers were recently accepted by the Government is intituled "Support for Self-employed Persons".

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: And as the recommendations themselves make clear, we have focused on the risks of self-employment that have been laid bare and exacerbated in recent years by the gig economy, such as unstable income that can fluctuate much more sharply and quickly than for more traditional self-employed persons outside the gig economy, such as stallholders in a hawker centre.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: And the group includes substantial numbers among the lower-income, more vulnerable groups in our population.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Because of the temporary and uncertain nature of gigs, these workers are more likely to be living from pay cheque to pay cheque and finding their short-time cash flow needs often trump their longer-term economic interest in saving for future retirement.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The question is, how can we provide them with better support, including through income tax amendments?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: With "deduct as you go" and consequently with smaller pay cheques, it is likely that short-term cash flow crunches will get worse for the gig economy workers, making it even more difficult and challenging for him or her to make voluntary Central Provident Fund (CPF) contributions in a disciplined way.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: As the Government studies the implementation of "Contribute-As-You-Earn", may I urge that it also look into tax incentives for self-employed persons to encourage them to make voluntary CPF contributions that will help with their retirement adequacy in future?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: I urge the Government to examine more generally the overall regime of tax incentives faced by gig economy workers.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Let us help this growing and often vulnerable group of workers with the support and protection that they, their dependants, their work and their enterprise deserve.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I will discuss how, in my view, this Bill achieves these objectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The tax reform that will probably affect the most Singaporeans is the change in tax treatment of PHC drivers' income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Hon Members and the public have asked for PHC drivers to be treated like taxi drivers for tax purposes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: At this point, I wish to declare my interest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I am a director of the Singapore Taxi Academy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Now, the basic problem is that PHC drivers are taxed on revenue and not their net income presently.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Since car operating costs are high in Singapore, their effective tax rate is much higher than it should be, given their net income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Today, PHC drivers can already deduct the commissions which are about 20% of fare revenue, on average.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But even with these deductions, they would pay from about $2,000 to $6,000 in annual income tax.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If we assume that drivers' net income is about 40% of gross revenue, the average tax rate for the more successful drivers could reach 12% of their net income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is an annual savings that is just like one month’s bonus for the drivers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But, Sir, is this a handout, a subsidy of some type that is costing the taxpayer?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is actually a reform that improves the efficiency of the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: After-tax earnings should reflect the economic value of the work done.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is not efficient to tax PHC drivers more than we tax taxi drivers when they do the same kind of work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Tax reforms like this will encourage Singaporeans to seek the most productive types of work, and reduce the chance that their work decisions are distorted by the tax system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The scope and nature of work is changing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We are seeing an unprecedented shift away from full-time employment into alternative, flexible forms of work, such as freelancing and contract work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Economists Alan Krueger and Lawrence Katz show in a paper forthcoming in the Industrial and Labor Relations Review, that the proportion of US workers in alternative work rose from 10.7% to 15.8%, from 2005 to 2015.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This was an increase of 23,400 workers between 2016 and 2017.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Are the incentives right, so that Singaporeans neither rush to alternative work, nor do they shy away from it?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Bringing this back to the Tax Bill, one area we could consider for tax reform is to ensure employees and the self-employed are treated the same when it comes to social security costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Many full-time employees are covered by company group health insurance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The company deducts the medical costs as business expenses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Except for MediSave, the self-employed do not enjoy tax deductions for personal medical costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, the problem is: employees effectively pay for medical costs from their pre-tax income, but the self-employed pay for it from post-tax income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Although CPF contributions are not a tax, I do beg your indulgence to touch on this briefly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Retirement and housing are also very important social security costs and CPF contributions are tax deductible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, the self-employed are not required to contribute to their CPF Ordinary and Special Accounts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: They, therefore, earn higher take-home incomes, which may appear to make alternative work more attractive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But, unfortunately, a wide body of research in behavioural economics suggests that people react to taxes and contributions which are visible or salient and they underreact to or ignore those which are not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A paper by Congdon, Kling and Mullainathan published in 2009 in the National Tax Journal provides a very good non-technical summary of this kind of research.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The problem is that take-home income is salient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The benefits of being an employee are not salient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The value of company-provided medical benefits, annual leave, staff training and so on are not salient to workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The value of CPF contributions, which provide for the social security of our workers, are not salient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Income taxes and the benefit of income tax deductions are also not salient because our system charges taxes the year after income is earned.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: On balance, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I believe alternative work, which fills your wallet with take-home income today, may sometimes be too attractive, especially for younger Singaporeans who may be tempted to forgo starting formal careers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And our tax system has a role to play in adjusting this balance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Taken together, Mr Deputy Speaker, we must continue the work of restructuring our tax system for the future economy to ensure the incentives are right for all workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In the future economy where income and jobs may vary highly year to year, we should seriously consider a pay-as-you-earn or contribute-as-you-earn income tax system, which will help to smooth take-home income for workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We may even enlist the help of the alternative work platforms to arrange for these tax deductions and contributions to be made at the source, when income is earned.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: These are issues for another day, of course.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I am in support of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is an issue I, along with several other Members of this House, have raised previously and I am glad that we are finally levelling the playing field and ensuring that it is fair.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I would first like to declare my interest as the Chief Executive of an IPC.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My interest notwithstanding, I support this extension in the spirit of giving and fostering a sense of community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Charities rely heavily on public donations, which empower us to make a difference in the community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The donations are our lifeline and, to be honest, fundraising remains a challenge for many of us, especially in recent times.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With this extension of tax deduction, I believe we can encourage more Singaporeans to give back and strengthen our community by donating more on issues we care about.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This deduction has been extended multiple times since it was first introduced as a temporary measure in 2009.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would send a stronger statement of the Government’s commitment to support voluntary giving.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It would also give the IPCs some greater assurance and stability.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Scheme complements the tax deduction for qualifying donations by encouraging employee volunteerism through businesses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would the Minister similarly consider formalising the 250% deduction for businesses' expenditure when employees volunteer and provide services to IPCs?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would the Minister also consider extending the scope of the Scheme?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have two suggestions on how this Scheme might be expanded.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, owners of the businesses, such as sole-proprietors, partners and shareholders who are also directors of the same company, are not qualifying employees under this Scheme.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify the rationale for this exclusion, and would the Minister consider extending the Scheme to owners of businesses?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Business owners volunteering their own time and services can send a very strong message on the value of volunteerism to their employees.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, could the Scheme be extended to charities that do not have IPC status?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: IPC status allows charities to issue deductible receipts for qualifying donations to donors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As the Scheme pertains to giving through acts of volunteerism rather than monetary donations, expanding this scheme to non-IPC charities would not blur the fundamental distinction between IPC and charities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: IPCs are rightfully held to a higher standard of compliance and governance, which not all charities have the resources to meet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, non-IPC charities continue to serve equally worthwhile causes and employees should be encouraged to volunteer with non-IPCs as much as with IPCs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this regard, there does not seem to be a good reason for drawing a distinction between the two.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, clauses 2(b), 3, 41, 42, 45, 46 and 47 propose to enhance IRAS’ powers to investigate tax crimes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I support the intention and agree with the need to take a whole-of-Government approach to crack down on tax crimes, given the increasing sophistication with which these crimes are carried out.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is also stated that “These powers under the proposed amendments will be exercised only by trained IRAS investigation officers and where necessary so that investigations are not impeded.” Could the Minister clarify what such training entails and share what safeguards are in place to prevent abuse of powers by IRAS officers?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand the Minister has replied to some of these in his opening speech.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will these officers undergo training similar to what our Police Officers go through?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand the Minister earlier mentioned that they undergo similar training to what our Singapore Customs officers go through.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, why not training that our Police Officers go through instead?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Deputy Speaker, I rise in support of this Bill which I note is giving more powers to investigators who are working to pursue those who are trying to evade paying taxes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is important that the investigation team be given more powers because, in today’s context, taxation is more complex.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These criminals can be involved in major crime syndicates, including terrorist groups.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I do not know whether the IRAS will be building up a new talent pool of investigators who will be armed under special circumstances, just as they do in the US Inland Revenue Service.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Or would IRAS tap on the Commercial Affairs Department (CAD) or other agencies and appoint them as "specially authorised officers" under the proposed amendments to support them in any raids done on the premises?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And what about interrogation rooms and holding centres where these arrested culprits are required to be held over a period while investigations are ongoing?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, I will move on to the amendment affecting PHCs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The shared economy is an increasingly global phenomenon and, as more PHC services continue to take interest in our market, we can only expect this industry to grow.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is important to constantly review and improve the current infrastructure to ensure that the trend is moving in a positive direction.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Changing the tax regime is one way to keep moving ahead.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I do not wish to make this issue into a case of taxi drivers versus PHC drivers because, in essence, allowing PHC drivers to claim tax deductions for expenses incurred on the job is simply about ensuring fairness.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: PHC drivers incur costs while providing an integral transportation service for the masses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is only right that they are able to claim for operating expenses, just like other businesses and service providers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would like now to share some examples of my residents who find themselves in predicaments because of the existing tax regime.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One resident had been involved in three road accidents, resulting in three periods of downtime, during which he was unable to drive and earn an income.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, he was still required to pay for the rental of the car due to the contract that he signed with the rental company.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This has resulted in an unfair situation where he has to pay for the job.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Meanwhile, another resident was having financial difficulties because not only does he find his tax liability too high, he also finds it a massive burden having to contribute to MediSave based on his inflated income, leaving him with little available income and cash to spare.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In another case, a resident's circumstances are even more dire.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have written to IRAS on behalf of these residents.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A common impression about PHC drivers is that many of them have dual jobs, and are driving part-time to supplement their incomes, or to pay off vehicle ownership.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Then there is the controversy of the seating preference.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For instance, a small number of PHC drivers do not like to be seen as drivers; they prefer their passengers to sit in front.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, some have questioned why should they be allowed tax deductibles if they do not identify themselves as providers of a professional service?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The reality is, I have met a number of residents who are full-time PHC drivers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They are driving full-time to support families, or to bridge a period of unemployment while waiting to hear from potential employers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They will share their grievances about the high costs of rental and fuel, while the income from their labour is fully taxable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And there are many valid reasons for them to stay as PHC drivers instead of switching over to a taxi company.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The most obvious one is age, and certainly some of them are not yet 30 years old trying to do something constructive while looking out for other career options, juggling housing loans and family commitments.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Then there are others who prefer the more flexible mileage requirements of PHC companies because they need to work longer hours, or the flexible hours are necessary to perform caregiving duties and so on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And for taxi drivers who are previously deterred by the difference in the income tax regime, this would give them additional options, and having options is always a good thing for the future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Of course, the other concern is that those who are working as PHC drivers are part of the gig economy that provides an income in exchange for labour, but this does not come with the typical benefits that are seen in full-time employment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Moreover, it is difficult for drivers to upskill and enhance their career portfolio in this industry.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: By amending the Income Tax regime in their favour, are we encouraging PHC drivers to remain where they are?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It will be good for everyone if the Minister could clarify whether there are plans to restrict the age limit.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will there be requirements for PHC drivers to undergo medical health screening to ensure that they are fit and healthy in the interest of public safety?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In my opinion, it is important to help make the jobs of PHC drivers affordable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They are providing a rather important service and they deserve a fairer tax regime.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the meantime, we must think of ways to help PHC drivers transit from the industry into another industry that they choose, if they wish to do so, and encourage them to keep on upskilling, but I suppose this would be a matter for another occasion, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The total tax deductible donations received by IPCs from corporate and individual donors have risen by 26% from about $687 million in 2008 to $866 million in 2016.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, this is a very encouraging trend and we hope more can continue to come forward to give.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Many donors contribute out of passion and heart for the community, and it is not just because of the tax incentives.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Having said that, the 250% tax deduction that we offer today is already one of the most generous tax deduction schemes worldwide.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Countries like Hong Kong, America and Australia provide only 100% tax deductions for corporate and individual donations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we do not think it is necessary at this stage to make this tax deduction permanent.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will continue to study ways to encourage giving, taking into account the needs and maturity of the charity sector, the impact of tax deductions on donations and the tax revenue forgone.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We also need to consider how the different deductions and reliefs benefit taxpayers in different income tax brackets.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We want to encourage corporate giving, but we remain open to existing, new or different ways of doing so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, let us monitor the progress of this scheme and study how best to further encourage corporate giving.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if the scheme could be extended to allow for the wages of sole proprietors, partners and shareholders, essentially the business owners, to be claimable.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The rationale for the scheme is for our businesses to encourage their employees to contribute their skills and time to the IPCs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, the business owners of the company already benefit from the tax deduction given to their businesses when their employees volunteer in the IPCs under this scheme.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked if the scheme could be extended to charities which are non-IPCs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Currently, only IPCs can issue tax-deductible receipts for qualifying donations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is so because IPCs are subject to stricter standards in regulatory compliance and governance, compared to the non-IPC charities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We apply the same standards for BIPS as wages and related expenses associated with volunteering are also eligible for tax deductions, and we will continue to review how to make this scheme accessible and relevant to encourage corporate volunteering.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, that is on the tax deductions for qualifying donations as well as the extension of BIPS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, let me touch on tax deduction for motor car-related expenses for PHC drivers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As many Members mentioned just now, many of you have spoken up about the need for the tax deduction.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have taken in your feedback, reviewed this extensively and we are now making these changes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The tax changes update our tax regime in view that taxi and PHC drivers now provide similar point-to-point transport services.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked about the difference between part-time and full-time PHC drivers and whether some of them would have difficulties apportioning their expenses correctly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, those who drive more would claim more, while those who drive less will claim less.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Nevertheless, drivers who still opt to claim tax deduction based on the actual amount of expenses incurred can do so if they wish to.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And if they want to do that, they will need to keep proper records of the expenses and ensure the correct apportionment of these expenses between that incurred to earn the driving income and that for private use.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I would imagine, with this deemed expense ratio, many drivers would consider using it for their convenience and for ease of compliance.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I would also like to clarify, in response to the question raised by Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, that currently, self-employed delivery persons are already allowed to claim tax deduction on expenses incurred on using motorcycles or commercial vehicles, such as vans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat shared about examples of residents who are PHC drivers who face difficulties in paying their income tax for YA2018 as well as their MediSave contributions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The tax changes will help them on a prospective basis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But for those individuals who may have difficulties with their existing obligations, I would advise that they contact IRAS and CPF Board, and the agencies will look into having a suitable instalment plan to assist them with their obligations, be it for tax or for MediSave contributions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat also asked about the regulations in respect of PHC drivers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: He asked about age limits, medical health certifications.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: All of these really come under the purview of MOT and the Land Transport Authority (LTA) which set the regulatory framework for PHC drivers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, LTA already requires all individuals to pass a medical examination before they can apply for their Private Hire Car Driver's Vocational Licence (PDVL), and I am sure these regulations will continue to be updated and reviewed by MOT and LTA.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Next, Assoc Prof Walter Theseira, Mr Chen Show Mao and Mr Saktiandi Supaat highlighted the need to consider this increase in people who are self-employed in light of the gig economy, and all of the Members rightly highlighted the concern that such self-employed persons may value more their take-home pay and put in less for their longer-term needs, be it for medical needs or for their retirement.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think Assoc Prof Theseira said this is actually a broader issue for another day, and truly it is, because it is a bigger issue than the amendments that are being contemplated in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Under this model, service buyers or intermediaries who contract with a self-employed person will deduct and transmit the MediSave contribution to the person's MediSave account whenever they pay a self-employed person.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This will allow the Government to work through the implementation issues and help smoothen its subsequent implementation in the private sector.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Of course, the issue is a far bigger one than just looking at the MediSave contributions alone, as many Members have highlighted.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we will continue to look at different options, including incentives where necessary, to better ensure the retirement adequacy of Singaporeans who are self-employed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Both Mr Louis Ng and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked some questions about IRAS' powers to investigate tax crimes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, let me just address some of the questions they have raised.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In general, investigations of tax offences are conducted by IRAS officers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In cases involving both tax evasion and other offences, such as money laundering or corruption, IRAS may engage the relevant agencies, be it CAD or the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau (CPIB), to conduct joint investigations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The training programmes are similar to that received by officers of other law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if it is similar to that of the Police Force because I only mentioned Customs as an example just now.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As mentioned earlier, the safeguards will be legislated to ensure that these enhanced investigative powers are properly exercised.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These safeguards are consistent with those applying to other law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In addition to these legislative safeguards, there will be clear guidelines and operational protocols on situations which allow for the exercise of these powers by authorised trained tax investigators.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Together, these measures will ensure that the enhanced investigative powers are properly calibrated and only exercised when other means are found to be inappropriate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about interrogation rooms and holding centres for suspects.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are already interview rooms in IRAS currently specifically catered for the questioning of suspects.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In situations where the subject under investigation is required to be held for a longer period, he or she may be escorted to facilities in the Police Force.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: MOF will continue to review our tax regime and our schemes regularly to ensure their relevance and effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The changes to the tax regime for PHC drivers and enhancements to IRAS' investigative powers are the results of such policy reviews.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have taken in their feedback, we have put in place these changes and I believe they are for the better.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair again at 4.25 pm.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.03 pm until 4.25 pm.
